A skill is a goal-driven capability with why it matters and the mastery and date it targets; it spans many life domains (physical, mental, spiritual, career, finance and the others), each one a tag, so everything related to the skill is tracked down across Vida.
Target mastery is a Purposes target, the pursuable that carries the measurement kind and binding mode; Purposes reads a skill's mastery live through Skills and keeps no copy.

Evidence (a project, a recording, a certificate) proves mastery through pages, attachments and deliverables, and a dev-log's key insights become Knowledge objects, created through Knowledge's service, in the user's principles store.

Skills' names and free text (a skill's name, description and why it matters, a level's criteria, indicators, challenges and key skills, an activity's instructions, prerequisites and success criteria, a dev-log's reflections and insights, the measurement config) are encrypted client-side; enums, dates, ratings and counters stay plaintext.
Skills composes the other modules' entities instead of rebuilding them and adds only the syllabus, the deliverables, the Composer and the graph, never parallel machinery.

Datasets and community templates arrive by a device-mediated public-reference whole-set fetch under the external-in grant, add-only, revocable and normalized per source, and the server never proxies it; a model draft is a scoped generate on the device or in the cloud as egress, never an agent, imported content carries its provenance into any prompt, and generated rows carry the ai source.

A skill incorporates any entity in any module as a component (habits, exercises and workouts, meals, Finance items, purposes, projects, books to read, programs and courses to take, Knowledge, sessions, tasks), many per skill, through entity links and never limited by a resource type; every Skills entity (`skill`, `skill_level`, `skill_activity`, `skill_dev_log`, `skill_dependency`) is in turn a target of tags, notes, pages and links, a practice being reached through its base session, and Skills owns no tag or link table.

A dev-log is the reflection on a practice session (how it felt, what worked, what to improve, the next plan, key insights), and Skills uses Health's adaptation engine as an integration, as it uses the other modules, so a skill can run experiments on the user's own learning; it reads the session's date and length instead of storing them.

Skills builds on other modules' entities instead of copying them; practice is a session of the practice sub_type, an assessment is a task of a Skills type, a study activity is a Knowledge study session and a project activity a Projects project, each anchored to its place in the syllabus and tracked Skills' way with what the base lacks, and habits, routines and the other modules attach and link to Skills entities.

The user prepares inside Skills following its syllabus; preparation (the practice cadence, reminders, and sessions scheduled automatically before a level's target, a deliverable's date or the target mastery date) is set on a skill and passed down to its levels, units, deliverables and components, and any entity below can override it; Sessions generates the sessions as planned blocks next to the other modules' entities.

Skills runs no due lane of its own; its due items ride their base entities, so practice is due as a planned session, an assessment as a task and decay maintenance as a review on Knowledge's lane, and they reach Today, the Calendar and reminders like any session, task or review.

Each skill defines its own ladder as data, ordered levels with completion criteria and success indicators, never one universal scale; ladder templates (belts, ranks, milestones, language levels) seed a ladder from a template or an opt-in dataset.

Skills ships the practice sub_type fully configured and registers it with Sessions; every practice is a session the user can name and type, attached to its activity, so the agenda and a routine step drive it.

Skills exposes its skills, levels, deliverables and activities and their events (a level reached, a deliverable done, a practice done or missed, a skill at risk of decay) and measures (level, progress, mastery, practice consistency) as measurement sources and rule subjects that Purposes and Gamification read live; nothing copies Skills' data.
A level-up, a mastery reached and a practice streak emit `award_xp` with no payload, and Gamification's handler applies the amount; Skills emits the signal and never writes points.
Skills contributes its day to the journal (practice done, levels reached, deliverables done, skills at risk), read live through its contribution.

Skills has its own journal blocks and capability blocks, the syllabus view, the life skill tree over the graph and a view of the user's skills across their domains among them; each reads Skills live and writes only through Skills' service, separate from its journal contribution.
Skills serves a read provider for its entity types, so links, views, the graph and search resolve a skill, level, unit, deliverable, activity or dev-log through Skills.
When the root composes Skills, Skills registers its practice sub_type and task types, its measurement sources, its journal contribution and its read provider; nothing is wired centrally.

Skill syllabus templates (levels, units, deliverables and suggested components), a starter skill graph with shared foundational skills, ladder templates, their locale variants and curated resources ship as opt-in default datasets the user accepts or declines, refreshed as a whole set and read from a local copy, filling and connecting the skills the user composes; the pattern is built even when declined.

The data model's record shows the Skills tables migration 021 built (seven tables, no foreign keys, the practice extension excluded from the entity types and without deleted_at, the resource junction retired, the older stored mastery default resolved out).

Skills' surfaces show every capability's terminal states (a skill planning, active, maintaining or completed, a Composer setup quick, advanced or incomplete, a fill by hand, from a template or dataset, drafting or failed, a level upcoming, active or complete, a deliverable open or done, a practice planned, in progress, complete or skipped, mastery with too little data, derived or overridden, a graph with no edges, a recommended path or a synergy, a decay flag none, at risk or dismissed).

The user composes each skill; there is no canonical definition library; a skill, its syllabus and its components fill by hand, from a template (save as template, create from template), from an opt-in dataset, or with an opt-in model draft, and Vida never submits to a community, the user's own template export being the only bridge.

A skill is organized by its own syllabus, shaped like Learning's hierarchy, the skill, its levels or stages and the units under them, with every component, activity and deliverable placed where the syllabus puts it and never free of its parent, so the user plans the skill and then follows it.

Each stage of a syllabus has Skills' own deliverables, shaped like Projects', a required output that holds its own tasks and measures, where only what's nested in a deliverable counts toward it, and deliverables track the skill's progress; an assessment, a task of a Skills type (SK-17), can be one of a deliverable's tasks.

Mastery and progress derive on read from the syllabus, its level gates and deliverables, and each component's own measures read live (a habit's adherence, a workout's records, a book's progress, a course's grade, Knowledge mastery, practice consistency), weighted as the user set them in the Composer; an ability that can't be measured digitally is qualitative, self-rated or evidence-based, a manual override is flagged, and Vida never fakes a number.

In the Skill Composer the user defines each skill, picks the entities from any module it incorporates and where each sits in the syllabus, what's tracked and how each counts toward progress and mastery (a measurement kind with derived-pull binding, referenced and never stored as a pursuable column), in a quick mode from a template or dataset or an advanced custom mode.

An activity's type sends its work to the owning module and anchors the entity there to its place in the syllabus; practice is a session, study a Knowledge study session on the skill's compound set, a project a Projects project, an assessment a task of a Skills type linked to Knowledge, and a review the review engine; any other entity joins the skill as a linked component, and Skills orchestrates like Routines.
A practice action is a session of the practice sub_type with Skills' one-to-one extension, the base session owning time and lifecycle, and practice time derives from the sessions.

The user's skill graph links their skills by requires, unlocks and synergy edges, and an opt-in dataset contributes a starter graph with shared foundational skills that the user incorporates; the graph recommends a path and detects synergies between goals.
An unpracticed skill decays through the review engine's curve, and its maintenance due item and reminder are advisory, configurable per skill and never nagging.

A tag attaches to any entity in Vida through one universal entity_tags primitive; there is no page-only tag path and no per-module tag table, and tagging and untagging are idempotent by business key, reviving a soft-deleted row and soft-deleting on remove.

A type groups a module's entities so they're tracked together, nest their information and get their own capabilities; types are life groupings (finances, relationships, spiritual life, family, health and more) that serve every module, Spaces owns the grouping and the user creates types through it, the base module owns the type's discriminator and the domain module owns its extension.
The user sets how tags and links interact (unified or separate) in a surface, and the switch is persisted; the resolution service stays stateless.

Spaces serves its reads (list and get a Space, its views, its palette and its contents), so the shell scope, nav and every surface can address a Space; nav placement and per-Space visibility are Preferences'.
A Space reads its contents and their progress live through each module's read providers and measures; it stores no copy of another module's data.
A Space has its own blocks, the way modules do; its day block shows what to do today in that Space, drawn from its member modules' due items and blocks, and it works for every Space.

The composition root builds the whole Spaces module (the views engine and its shared provider registry, the association resolver, the templates service, the capability registry, enforcer and offered set) and each module registers its taggable types, read providers and template writers when it's composed.
ADR-002 records the Spaces module's tables (tags, entity_tags, entity_links, spaces, space_enabled_blocks, views, templates, capability_definitions, block_instances, capability_grants) as built.

Taggable and linkable entity types come from one open registry; a module makes its entities taggable by registering a type, never by a schema edit, and an unregistered type is refused with a typed error.
Tags nest through a parent tag, so a Space sub-groups (#languages contains #languages/spanish); a tag's name and description are user content, and a nesting cycle is refused.

Tags (grouping) and links (typed reference) stay two tables drawing on the one registry, and Vida resolves an entity's associations into one unified space or two separate ones on the user's choice, a real behavioral resolution over untouched storage.

A Space is a first-class spaces record (root tag, name, icon, default view, offered palette, parent Space), nav-addressable and nestable, not just a tag; its contents are everything carrying its root tag, and a nesting cycle is refused.
A Space's offered palette is a stored set of capability definitions (space_enabled_blocks), authored configuration distinct from its placements, never a projection over them.
Every Spaces-tier table syncs and soft-deletes, and tag, Space and link names, descriptions and contexts are encrypted client-side; in M1 encryption is a pass-through with an empty [E] set.

Spaces is the module where the user builds their own modules out of Vida's modules, bringing in other modules' entities, features and capabilities and connecting them into new features, then using them to personalize Vida; nothing a module owns is lost or copied along the way.
A Space makes something abstract real inside Vida, such as a language, family, work or church, by grouping the entities of every module that belong to it under its root tag.
A session is exactly one sub_type over one shared spine; pomodoro is the focus runtime, never a sub_type, and each owning module registers its own sub_type.
On completion the engine emits a signal (duration, resource, outcome); Knowledge owns mastery and Education owns pace, and Sessions never computes a domain measure.
Pomodoro is the focus sub_type's runtime, owned in the Sessions realm and keyed by session_id; the Notes /pomodoro block is a lens onto focus sessions, never the owner.
Session analytics (completion rate, average focus, planned-vs-actual, time per module, streaks) are derived on read from the session log, never stored in synced aggregate tables.
A dueIn provider lane that fails degrades only that lane with a typed ProviderUnavailable(module), the other lanes render, and the engine never writes another module's schedule to recover.

generatePlan(scope, window) plans across every module, not one course, and a batch travels draft, pending_approval, approved, active, then completed or failed; no availability or nothing to schedule fails explicitly (NoAvailability, NothingToSchedule), never as an empty batch.
A planned block whose target due work vanished before it ran resolves to empty and is dropped or flagged, never left as a dangling row.
A session with ended_at before started_at, or a duration beyond its block window, is a typed validation error and is never stored.
Editing a shipped type is allowed behind a not-recommended warning, scoped to the user's device and never pushed as a default.
Sessions has its own view family (Hub, wizard, Management, Availability, per-type tools) and an empty state that offers a starter availability grid and the shipped types.
An effect whose attached entity was deleted no-ops loudly with a typed AttachmentTargetMissing; it never resurrects the entity or fails the whole completion.
sub_type (the tool family and owner) and purpose (why) are separate axes and separate enums, never one conflated enum.

Every completion goes through one door, transition(), which checks that every declared non-projection effect has a handler before any write (NoEffectHandler), treats a soft-deleted session as missing, and counts as fired only the effects the ledger applied.
Whether a completed session's effects were applied is derived on read from the applied_effects ledger, never stored as a flag, and a replay re-applies only the effects with no ledger row.
Sessions ships the study sub_type, fully configured in all four dimensions, as the scheduling engine's own generated sessions; focus and study are the shipped roster.
No session type, shipped or user-made, exists without all four Integration Contract dimensions declared (attachment, effects, lifecycle, permissions).
Every identified sub_type ships fully configured by us; the user never sets up the main ones, and user extensibility is for new long-tail types only.
A user-created type may attach to any entity and declare effects only inside its permission envelope, and sensitive-module effects (Finance, Health) need explicit opt-in consent.

A session never affects an entity it is not attached to, two types never count the same event twice (deterministic effect_event_id over the applied_effects ledger), and a permission violation is a hard, logged rejection.
The engine owns planned_blocks and its own generated sessions but never stores a copy of another module's due work; the agenda is its own blocks plus live dueIn provider reads.
A planned_block is the plan and never the log; completing it calls the owner's createSession(), which carries planned_block_id.
Availability windows and exceptions are Planner-owned scheduling input; Routines may preset recurring windows, and attended sessions consume availability while planned ones fill it.

Vida runs as three product shapes, the localhost web product on the user's machine with all data local and no server, the server product the user hosts, and the desktop and mobile apps, and every rule that depends on where Vida runs names the shape it means.
Every last-writer-wins stamp is a hybrid logical clock stamp, never a bare wall clock, so a device with a skewed clock corrects itself on its next merge.
Every synced table carries the sync columns and a per-field stamp map; the sync queue, the search index and app_state stay on their device and never sync.

A base row and its extension row travel together; a device applies an extension only once its base is present, a base without its extension renders as a valid, tool-less entity, and the writer queues both at once.

Structured changes push two seconds after the last write, on reconnect, on a manual sync and every five minutes while open, pulling when a mobile app comes to the front; page content syncs every five seconds while edited, on leaving the page and on save; attachments upload when added.
Changes move over one authenticated socket per user with a 30-second heartbeat and reconnect backoff up to 30 seconds, falling back to polling every 60 seconds while the socket is down.

Offline, everything works but sync and uncached attachments; the queue survives restarts, and on reconnect the device pushes its queue in order, pulls what changed since its last sync, merges and records the new sync time on the device.

The server signs the user in, stores each encrypted blob and page snapshot, relays a push to the user's other online devices, keeps an ordered change feed per user for pulls, serves attachments by signed link, keeps the device registry, sends the content-free wake signal and deletes soft-deleted blobs after 30 days.
With the server product, the user's own server serves the web app, so the user opens Vida from their server; the localhost web product keeps its static build.

The server is open source and self-hostable first; a relay Victor hosts later is an option, never required, and device limits and billing apply only to that hosted relay, never to a self-hosted server.

Each device generates its id once and keeps it on the device; its first sign-in registers it on the server with its name and platform, and the user lists, renames and sees when each device was last seen.
The device is the source of truth; every write succeeds locally first, sync is an eventual copy between the user's devices and never a dependency, and the server stores and relays but never merges.

Revoking a device closes its connection, tells the other devices and refuses its sign-in, without erasing the data already on it, and Vida points the user to changing the password, which re-keys the vault.

A new device signs in, unlocks the vault and pulls the profile, preferences and app configuration before it opens, then the last 30 days in the background by table priority with visible progress, then the rest in resumable batches of 100, leaving attachments until opened and rebuilding search at the end.

The user exports all their data on the device, decrypted and with no server, as one file per table, pages as Markdown and attachments as their files in one archive, which is also the backup and the way into the encrypted app.

The account is the user's identity across their own devices, never an account with Vida as a company; it holds their contact details, the password and authentication that unlock Vida, and the devices signed in.

With a server, signing in on a new device connects to the user's own server and brings their data in; without one, the account lives on the device, its details plus the password that unlocks the vault there.
The account's contact details are stored in the user's profile, Settings shows the account without owning its data, and the System panel's Account entry opens it.
Signing in to the server uses the secure remote password protocol, so the server keeps only a salt and a verifier and never sees a password or a key.

The account lets the user sign out of a device and delete the account; deleting removes both the user's data on their server and the vault on the device, offers a backup first, and runs only after the user confirms and types a phrase that clearly states they want the account deleted.

The desktop app runs the same web codebase with a native, encrypted SQLite store behind the shared database adapter, an addition rather than a rewrite, and adds a tray, global shortcuts, auto-update, file system access for attachments and export, and native notifications.

The mobile app shares the core and the interface, runs the editor, charts and graph inside web views with native chrome around them, and adds push, haptics, a share sheet, biometric unlock and background sync.
Sync copies one user's data across that user's own devices; there is no sharing between users, no presence and no shared cursors.
The localhost web product keeps its database in the browser's private file store with no server, so its data lives in that browser and the whole-vault export is its safety copy.
A replayed blob is refused, by the server on a lower version and by the device on an older stamp.

The server is blind; it stores and relays only encrypted blobs and never decrypts, indexes, queries, links or merges them, and the plain header it reads (table, row, version, clock stamp, device, operation and the changed field names) is the disclosed limit of what it learns.
Sync to a server turns on only after the encryption pass, so before it each device's data stays on that device.

Each row of a synced table is one sync unit, serialized whole, compressed and encrypted into one blob whose plain header carries each changed field's clock stamp, so a device can merge per field before it decrypts.

A page's content syncs as its own Yjs document, the server keeping only the latest full snapshot, beside the page's metadata as a row blob; content merges without conflicts, and the page's stored content is a snapshot rebuilt after each merge.

On the device a file is stored encrypted on its own row in the device's database; across devices it syncs apart from the row queue, at most 25 megabytes, uploaded through a short-lived signed link while its metadata syncs last-writer-wins, downloaded only when opened and kept on the device, and deleted on the server 30 days after its row.

Structured data merges per field, last writer wins by clock stamp with the higher device id breaking an exact tie; the id, sync id and creation time never merge, updated_at takes the merge's wall-clock time, and a delete is an ordinary field, so a delete and an edit resolve by their stamps.
Until sync is activated, the sync engine does no network I/O; its flush loop exists but every transport, push and pull step is inert, so nothing leaves the device.

The engine only consumes the sync queue; the entity write and its queue row are written together by the repository, and the engine reads pending rows and, once activated, moves their status or removes them after the server acknowledges.
A queued payload arrives already encrypted, and the engine treats it as an opaque blob it never decrypts, inspects or re-encrypts.
Pending queue rows drain first in, first out, by when they were queued.
Repeated edits of a row before a flush coalesce to its latest snapshot, and a create followed by a delete of the same row collapses to nothing before any push.
The queue's status (pending, in flight, failed) and a row's own sync status (pending, synced, conflict) are two separate states, and the queue reader moves only the queue's.

A failed push retries with backoff from 1 to 30 seconds up to three times, then is marked failed and shown as changes that failed to sync with a manual retry; a client error is never retried, an authentication error stops all sync and asks the user to sign in again, and an encryption error stops only that blob.
The field-level merge and the per-page Yjs merge are reserved seams with their final interfaces, and nothing merges until sync is activated.
Activating sync fills the reserved seams with no schema change and no change to any consumer.
A task's title, description and tag associations are encrypted client-side [E]; status, priority, difficulty, dates and estimates are plaintext config. M1 is a pass-through.
Every create, edit, complete and timer action succeeds locally first with a co-transactional sync_queue row, and structured columns reconcile Last-Writer-Wins across devices.

A task is a pursuable with measurement_kind (natural milestone) and binding_mode (completion is the event trigger); it stores no progress column, is never an M5 measure source, and contributes up to a purpose only through contributions.

Deleting a parent module's entity (project, milestone, course or contact) asks the user what happens to its tasks, deleting them with it, unlinking them into standalone tasks, or moving them to another entity, either nested inside it (a milestone) or at its top level; tasks are never deleted silently.
A project, course or contact page lists its tasks through the Tasks service by its parent link, never a table read; Tasks serves the read port Projects declares (listProjectTasks, getFocusMinutes).

A focus run bound to a task writes its real minutes into the task's one ledger through attach_pomodoro and log_time, the same ledger the work timer writes (TK-5's deferred task_time_logs and session reconciliation).

Completing a task grants experience points through `award_xp`, applied by Gamification as `grant_currency(XP)` into the consequence_ledger; one task grants once, ever, each obligation occurrence grants anew, and Tasks never writes points itself.

A task's completion emits emit_measurement_signal for the measurement engine and pushes nothing to Purposes; a purpose, goal or dream a task relates to reads it through the Tasks service and computes it into that day's progress.
The journal's daily summary pulls the tasks completed, due or scheduled on the day through the Tasks journal contribution; Tasks never pushes surface_journal.
A task's scheduled_date is the planned work date, distinct from due_date; both feed Today, the Calendar and the Sessions due-work lane, with the deadline carried as hard_deadline.

The All-Tasks screen hosts the base task layouts as selectable renderers over one saved-view config, with a view-builder that saves named views rows (filter, layout, grouping), global or Space-owned, and offers a preset when no custom view exists.

A task sets at most one of project_id, milestone_id, course_id and contact_id, and a milestone implies its project; two parent FKs are a typed MultipleParentError, and a task with none is a first-class standalone task.
The twelve task layouts map onto the seven ADR-007 view layouts as layout, filter and grouping configs, and no task_views table exists.
A task preset is Spaces' tab over a task type (a saved views config plus per-type defaults), bound to the type Tasks defines (TK-27); the preset never owns a discriminator of its own.
The user pins and reorders saved task views per Space, stored by Preferences as per-view nav placement and read by the Tasks view switcher.
The task detail shows the task's fields, its sub-tasks with the rollup, its time logs and timer, its linked note and its focus runs; a sub-task is created only through addSubtask.

Every Tasks surface renders its terminal states (task list or view, create and edit, sub-task rollup, timer, obligation completion, view-builder); a failed save or timer action reverts and shows a typed error, and an obligation that can't regenerate completes and is flagged.

React Query owns task reads and writes, with optimistic create, edit and complete that show at once and revert on failure, and paginated lists for large sets; Zustand owns the ephemeral screen state (active view, view-builder draft, running timer, board drag, selection). The /tasks route's invalidate-and-reread is replaced.

Tasks has its own block, the task checklist, an inline capability entry; it lists tasks filtered by project, milestone, deliverable or due date with its terminal states, reads Tasks live, and ticks, unticks and creates tasks only through the Tasks service; on a journal page it shows that day's tasks through the Tasks journal contribution.

Tasks owns a type registry beside the kind, holding shipped types, types modules register when composed (Health's exam and meal, Education's assessment and homework, Skills' assessment) and types the user creates through Spaces, each extended by its domain module keyed on the task.

Sub-tasks are one level; the parent shows the ADR-011 M4 weighted rollup of its children (per-child nesting weight, equal by default), derived on read with no stored progress, and completing a parent never completes its children, nor the reverse.
Deleting a task deletes its sub-tasks and its task_time_logs.

Time is one ledger; actual_minutes is the sum of the task's task_time_logs, written only by the log_time effect of the work session the timer opens, never a direct client write, and a task may opt out of time tracking (no logs, no rollup).

A task is complete when status is completed and completed_at is set, and reopening clears it; the completion is the task's event trigger and fires the S4 effects through the rail, idempotently, so in the app the tasks service is composed with the effect rail.

Only an obligation recurs; completing an obligation with a recurrence rule spawns exactly one next occurrence with the next due_date, even after a reopen and re-complete, and standard tasks never recur.
Tasks tag through the shared entity_tags primitive with entity_type task, never a private inline tag list.

The aggregated view reads only the tasks table and resolves parent-module data through the R7 read seam (the shared ViewProviderRegistry); a source that is down degrades only its own group, and standalone tasks form the Inbox group.

A template is a portable seed bundle of a Space's root tag, seed entities, views, offered capabilities with their config and child Space structure, a document with no live foreign keys; shipped templates are bundled assets and the user's are rows in a light templates store with no edit in place.
Creating from a template forks it, deep-copying the bundle into fresh entities that carry no template id, so template and instance never affect each other.

Saving a Space as a template captures only authored structure and configuration, never accumulated runtime data (logs, completions, entries, live entity ids), and a capability config that can only point at accumulated data is not capturable.

A preset is a type's tab, lighter than a template, made of a saved view over the type's entities plus per-type screens, default fields and deliverables and an optional starter template, owned by Spaces and bound to a type the base module defines.
Creating from a template ends in-progress, success or partial-failure; a bundle that names a capability missing on the device seeds what it can and flags the rest.
The user saves any Space as a template and creates a Space from one, through a writer each module registers for its entity types; an unregistered type is a partial failure.
Shipped templates and starter Spaces (the Languages starter, Health's training programs and the presets) come as opt-in datasets the user accepts or declines, read from a local copy.

Exporting and importing a template is the Integrations feature on the localhost product, which has no server; templates are Vida's only sharing bridge, and capability code arriving in an imported template is untrusted.
A saved surface is a views row (filter × layout × grouping and sort), not a component; the view components are the renderers a view selects.

A view is global (no Space) or owned by one Space, a Space may own many views and its default view names the one that opens first, and cloning a view makes an independent copy for a Space or the global set, with no back-link.

A view's layout is one of list, table, board, gallery, calendar, graph or timeline; filter, grouping and sort are stored as documents, a group-by field a row lacks goes to an ungrouped bucket, and a layout missing a field degrades, never crashes.

A cross-module view fans out to each entity type's registered read provider and merges the results, never reading another module's tables; a type with no provider degrades to a note and an empty contribution.
A view's name and the user-literal values in its filter are encrypted client-side, every view declares loading, empty, error and success, and a provider error resolves to error, never a crash.

listViews returns every live view in a stable order with no scoping on the primitive; a module scopes by its own identity rule, and pinning and ordering views in nav are Preferences', never a views column.
Vida ships a default set of views per entity type and per shipped Space, the user creates, edits and clones their own, and views help the user find their way around Vida.

A view's predicates follow one grammar (including a multi-tag intersection), each provider advertises the predicates it supports, and a predicate a provider doesn't support is ignored for that type, never silently dropping it, unless the view opts to exclude it.
Each layout declares the entity fields it needs, and the task layouts map onto the seven layouts as layout, filter and grouping configs.
